chunks: First: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman whom a man married, and she had a husband.

He said: Upon him is flogging, and upon her is stoning, because he had advanced with knowledge and she had advanced with knowledge. His expiation, if he does not present himself to the Imam, is to give charity with five sa's of fine flour.

Second: As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Shu'bi, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman who had a husband. He said: They are separated. I said: And upon him is beating? He said: No, why would he be beaten? So I left from his presence while Abu Basir was by the gutter, and I informed him of the question and the answer.

He said to me: Where am I? I said: By the gutter. He said: So he raised his hand and said: By the Lord of this House, or by the Lord of this Kaaba, I heard Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: Indeed Ali (peace be upon him) ruled in the case of a man who married a woman who had a husband, that he stoned the woman and gave the man the fixed punishment.

Then he said: If I had known that you knew, I would have smashed your head with stones. Then he said: What frightened me is that you might not have been given the knowledge, so you would not contradict what this narration contained of his saying: 'There is no beating upon him.' The first narration, because this narration is applied to one who does not know that the woman has a husband, and the first is inclusive of one who knew that, so the fixed punishment was upon him.

And he clarified that in the first narration when he said: 'Indeed he had advanced with knowledge and she had advanced with knowledge.' And upon this is applied what Abu Basir narrated at the end of the final narration from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his narration of the case of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), that he did that only for one who knew that she had a husband, so he gave him the fixed punishment.

And it is possible that the narration is applied to the fact that he only gave him the punishment which is the discretionary punishment (ta'zir), rather than the complete fixed punishment, and that is if it predominated in his opinion that she had a husband, so he was negligent in investigating that, and thus earned for this negligence the discretionary punishment.

And his saying (peace be upon him): 'If I had known that you knew, I would have smashed your head with stones,' the meaning is that if you knew with certainty that she had a husband, you would have done that. And it is permissible that that is specific to one who was suspected, who claimed that he did not know that, and no proof was established for him regarding the marriage, so the fixed punishment was upon him, which indicates that.

Third: What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), about a woman who married while she had a husband, he said: The woman is stoned, even if there is proof for the one who married her regarding her marriage, otherwise he is given the fixed punishment.
ai.seo_question: What is the punishment for a woman who marries while her husband is still alive according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* elucidates the jurisprudential distinction between *hadd* (fixed punishment) and *ta'zir* (discretionary punishment) in cases of *al-mu'ana* (a woman marrying while her previous husband is alive), relying on the principle of *khafa' al-yaqin* (doubt regarding certainty). The text reconciles apparent contradictions by attributing stoning to those with definitive knowledge of the existing marriage and flogging to those whose ignorance was excusable or whose status was merely suspected, a nuance highlighted by the Imam's reaction to the narrator's potential misunderstanding. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the precise conditions of knowledge (*'ilm*) and certainty (*yaqin*) in applying penal codes.
